newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Libya's Gaddafi defends Islam on Nigeria visit.
newsitem.headline: Libya's Gaddafi defends Islam on Nigeria visit.

text.p: Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi on Friday told a large crowd of worshippers in northern Nigeria that the West was tarnishing the image of Islam by portraying it as a terrorist movement.

Gaddafi, who flew in to an enthusiastic welcome in Kano in northern Nigeria where he led Moslem prayers, said the acts of violence that are taking place in Algeria are the work of an anti-Islamic movement.

"The whole world today is talking about Islam, giving a very tarnished picture of Islam and daily showing this tarnished picture...This propaganda is making people shun Islam", Gaddafi said in a speech broadcast live on Libyan television and monitored by the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC).

"Nowadays, they talk about Islam only when they talk about terrorism, killings, extremism, massacres. They mention examples of what is happening in Islamic countries like Algeria: the killing of women, children, the elderly, innocent people who are slaughtered with knives, and whose heads are severed with axes."

Gaddafi added: "I want to stress to the world today from the town of Kano, from the heart of Islam, from the heart of Africa, that what is happening in Algeria and the like is not Islamic extremism, Islamic violence or Islamic terrorism."

"What is happening in Algeria is being perpetrated by a movement that is anti-Islamic, outside Islam, a movement that is an enemy of Islam. This movement is called the heresy movement," said Gaddafi who is reportedly fighting an Islamist backlash in Libya for almost two years.

Gaddafi was addressing worshippers at the ultra-modern Kofar Mata mosque in Kano, the hometown of Nigeria's military ruler General Sani Abacha and northern Nigeria's biggest city. Nigeria is a secular state although the north is predominantly Moslem.
State radio said Gaddafi was accompanied by President Ibrahim Bare Mainassara of Niger, which he visited on Thursday at the start of a two-day controversial West African trip.
It said the two African leaders, who like their Nigerian counterpart are shunned by the West, would later hold talks on matters of common interest but did not elaborate.
Officials said Gaddafi would fly from Kano to the capital Abuja with his host Abacha for a state banquet.
Witnesses reported heavy security at Kano airport, where Gaddafi was met on arrival by Abacha, senior officials and local people.

Thousands of people lined the streets to the airport and Moslem youths carried banners with pictures of Gaddafi and Abacha. Journalists counted three Libyan planes at Kano airport and were not allowed on the tarmac where he disembarked.
Gaddafi was also accompanied by Libyan security men.
Gaddafi's trip to West Africa is in apparent defiance of a 1992 United Nations embargo on flights from his pariah state.
The ban was imposed for Libya's failure to extradite two agents linked to the bombing of the Pan Am flight over Lockerbie in 1988 and four agents linked to the 1989 bombing of a French airliner.

In Washington, a State Department spokesman said on Thursday the United States was investigating reports that the flight embargo had been broken and if it had been, the matter would be pursued in the U.N. Security Council and sanctions committee. A U.S. official said military action was not being considered.
Gaddafi's last trip abroad was by land to Tunisia in October 1996. He violated the ban when a Libyan-registered plane flew him to Cairo and back to attend an Arab summit in June 1996.
The Libyan news agency JANA on Wednesday said Gaddafi was visiting Niger and Nigeria as the leader of the Islamic Popular Leadership, an organisation he created in 1989.
Nigeria's Abacha has been shunned by the West since his 1993 coup after a previous military government annulled elections.
